t: Maximum Subtree of the Same Color
o: Root the tree at 0 and find the largest subtree whose nodes all share one color. A subtree rooted at v is monochromatic iff colors[v] matches every child's subtree color and each child subtree is itself monochromatic; its size is 1 plus the sizes of matching monochromatic child subtrees. Examples confirm sizes 1, 4, and 3 respectively.
k: Post-order DFS: a node's subtree is uniform iff all children subtrees are uniform with the same color as the node.
Size accumulates only from children that are uniform AND colored like the parent.
With n up to 5·10^4, use an iterative DFS to avoid recursion-depth crashes.

a.i: Build adjacency lists, run an explicit-stack DFS computing (uniform?, size) per node bottom-up, and track the maximum size among uniform nodes. Children results are combined at pop time after their pushes resolve.
s: DFS from root; on finishing node v, check each child c: uniform requires child uniform and colors equal.
size[v] = 1 + sum of matching uniform child sizes; update the global answer.
a.t: O(n) — each node pushed twice onto the stack

a.i: The same post-order logic written recursively is shorter and clearer; safe for typical test depths but risks stack overflow on degenerate chains in Python unless recursion limits are raised.
s: Track the max over uniform nodes.

c.python:
import sys
from typing import List
class Solution:
    def maximumSubtreeSize(self, edges: List[List[int]], colors: List[int]) -> int:
        sys.setrecursionlimit(200000)
        n = len(colors)
        adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for u, v in edges:
            adj[u].append(v); adj[v].append(u)
        self.ans = 1
        def dfs(v, p):
            sz, uni = 1, True
            for w in adj[v]:
                if w == p: continue
                cu, csz = dfs(w, v)
                if cu and colors[w] == colors[v]: sz += csz
                else: uni = False
            if uni: self.ans = max(self.ans, sz)
            return uni, sz
        dfs(0, -1)
        return self.ans

w: The iterative version is the safer interview answer for large n. Pitfall: a child subtree can be uniform yet a different color — it contributes nothing to the parent's size but doesn't invalidate itself. Edge cases: n = 1 (answer 1), star graphs. Follow-up: count uniform subtrees rather than the maximum size.
